comments.author: Jlannin
comments.body:
Some of the building blocks are already on newer iPhones. [Apple’s Foundation Models framework](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/09/apples-foundation-models-framework-unlocks-new-intelligent-app-experiences/) lets developers use the AI model built into Apple Intelligence directly inside a game. It's not Claude like in capabilities, but it runs on compatible devices without an internet connection or per-request AI fees. Apple even has a [sample game with generated NPCs and interactive conversations](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundationmodels/generate-dynamic-game-content-with-guided-generation-and-tools).

Where this gets interesting is connecting that AI to actions inside the game. An NPC could interpret what you say and respond through the game’s systems. I'm using it to enhance procedural effects with actually having an LLM create new assets with-in well defined guardrails. 

The fully open-ended version you’re describing is a much bigger challenge, especially keeping it coherent, responsive and fun. I’d expect this to arrive gradually rather than as one sudden next-generation leap.

replies.author: waypostmaster
replies.body: Could I somehow get that wired into an online game if I built an apple app for it?

replies.author: Jlannin
replies.body:
It’s really for games that run on Apple devices. Now you can literally make a game of any type, provided it has internet access, call an AI like Claude or OpenAI to do things. 

However there are potential real costs to do this which you have to pay for, especially for open ended use cases. 

Still, the basic pattern is emerging for building AI capabilities right into the flow of a game.

comments.author: cdcox
comments.body:
I can see a few concepts in there, some of which are pretty far off and some of which are almost here.

The first is something like a dynamic visual novel where you can do anything in am unconstrained way. And that already exists more or less. But it's not perfect. There are mods for silly tavern or similar tools that let you bring in a key, set up a world, set up rules, define NPCs, and essentially do anything you want with with realisticish but dynamic responses from the NPCs/world. If you're willing to wire in some image makers, text to speech, some basic rules, and a good enough model the whole thing can produce a nearly infinite game with nearly infinite assets, to the extent that a 2d visual novel has assets. Of course, these things eat tokens, but it's essentially an infinite game with realisticish characters. These tools exist right now but I think we're still a year or two out before we see a real game that takes this and does something awesome with it.

The second which someone already alluded to in the comments, is procedural generation in something like no man's sky. Essentially you have infinite levels and you can go anywhere and do anything there because it's all been procedurally generated. Of course the NPCs are extremely dumb/ non-existent and you still are always playing with the relatively limited rule set of no man's sky no matter where you go, so it's not like you really have that much freedom. Also, the content all feels pretty samey and unauthored.

The third is some sort of modification off the first which is like putting agents into an existing game framework. There are a number of mods that have started working with this with local or online models to give AI agents npcs realistic dialogues or more responsive behavior. At least I've seen mods for Skyrim and Morrowind that mess with this idea. They still operate within the rule set. But it begins to get to that semi-realistic companion thing. This technology is probably not there yet. The few mods that exist are kind of still pretty half-baked, I'm guessing a year before we get a good mod that does this well and maybe like two to three before we see it in a game. This also eats API tokens though sometimes works with local models. 

The 4th is a game that can expand within its own rule set. Think something like Baldur's gate that where you can go anywhere. Sort of a true DnD engine. A game essentially takes whatever you do and rolls with it, building new maps, new enemies having the world respond to you etc. combine that with some kind of free dialogue system and you could have a fairly dynamic story system. Of course, something like this would mostly exist within the rule set of where it starts. It would mostly be using something like mod tools to just build out as things go on. The difference vs procedural generation is that proc gen tends to produce somewhat repetitious and random content, whereas something like this could produce content that feels more authored and linked to an existing setup. I suspect we're probably 2 years from someone releasing something like this with a 2d game and maybe 3-5 years from someone releasing this with something 3D.  The issue is that asset generation is still extremely slow and these models are far too agreeable and not quite creative or good enough at writing yet. 

The last one which you're sort alluding to would be a game that can freely redesign itself and it's rules as you play with it. Like a game that writes code while you're playing it. Doing that live is probably borderline impossible. I think it would be more likely that something like a system where a game could maybe make modifications overnight might be more feasible. The problem is all coding agents currently produce an enormous amount of bloat and if you let something like this run free, you would almost certainly get a non-functional piece of software after a day or two. I'd be surprised if we see something like this before 2030. It's a difficult  ask and game systems often require a lot of testing to make sure new rules interacti in rhe correct way. It's one of the reasons a lot of the vibe coded games rarely evolve into real games. As you add more and more stuff you get things that are weirdly incompatible/buggy/slow. So you need a very disciplined agent or a programmer to keep them from bloating. I suspect something like this might not even be that fun really. I think games are more fun by their constraints. A game where you can kind of do anything is just writing a video game. At that point that's just a job. That being said, people like Minecraft and factorio so there's probably a market or something like this. But again, the agents we got just are not smart enough now.
